strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: there is no systematic benchmark for evaluating GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, and the proposed MAS-Bench is a well-motivated first step in this direction.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: 139 tasks across 11 real apps with an intentionally incomplete shortcut knowledge base forces agents to combine shortcuts with GUI operations, testing planning rather than mere shortcut lookup.

The two-stage framework for evaluating agent-generated shortcuts (generation stage + quality evaluation via a unified baseline agent) is a clever and fair methodology that isolates shortcut quality from agent capability.

The evaluation suite is multi-dimensional (7 metrics covering success, efficiency, cost, and shortcut-usage behavior), and the predefined-shortcut vs. replay vs. dynamic shortcut comparison yields informative findings about the brittleness of replay-style shortcuts.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: multiple agent architectures (T3A, M3A, MobileAgentV2, MobileAgent-E), two base models, difficulty-level breakdowns, and a qualitative failure analysis (Fig. 7) that provides useful taxonomy of shortcut-related errors.
Appendices provide substantial implementation detail (emulator configuration, action space, shortcut collection methodology, task breakdowns), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper claims to be 'the first benchmark' for shortcut-augmented agents, but this is overstated: existing systems (MobileAgent-E, AppAgentX, SkillWeaver) already evaluate self-generated shortcuts/skills, and Table 1's comparison with prior benchmarks is somewhat self-serving. The claim needs qualification.

Missing artifact link: the abstract states 'The project page is available at' but no URL is provided. For a benchmark paper, public release of the environment, task set, and shortcut KB is essential for reproducibility and community impact.

Results presentation has inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the abstract claims 64.1% vs. 44.6% GUI-only, but 44.6% corresponds to the weakest baseline (MobileAgentV2), not the GUI-only counterparts (T3A achieves 51.1%); Table 2 contains unexplained anomalies (e.g., M3A cross-app MSRS of 1.262 exceeding human-optimal; MobileAgent-E having low MSRS but very poor SR), and MET varies wildly across agents without discussion of what drives this.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported. With 139 tasks, differences such as 51.1% vs. 57.6% (T3A vs. MAS-T3A) may not be reliable; benchmark conclusions should not rest on single-run point estimates.

Potential confounds in the hybrid-agent comparisons are not controlled: MAS-MobileAgent injects retrieved shortcut descriptions into prompts, so performance gains may partly reflect prompt engineering rather than shortcut utility. The exact retrieval mechanism, prompt formats, and how the agent learns which shortcuts are applicable are underspecified in the main text.

The shortcut generation evaluation is conducted on only a 50% random task subset (69 tasks), and the generation method (M3A trajectory + LLM prompting) is a narrow slice of possible strategies; conclusions about 'substantial room for improvement' rest on limited evidence.
All main experiments use a single proprietary model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) with only one additional model for one comparison; generality of the benchmark across model families is unverified.

Several operational details are unclear: how 'success' is automatically verified for shortcut-augmented trajectories (the adaptation of SPA-Bench is only sketched), how optimal step counts for MSRS are computed, and whether API shortcuts that 'alter application state directly' reflect realistic usage or give agents unrealistic privileged access.
Writing has notable issues: broken citation ('et al., O. 2024'), placeholder-like text, and occasional overclaiming (e.g., 'pioneers', 'first framework') that a revision should temper.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and timely gap: there is no established benchmark for GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, and the two-stage evaluation protocol (agent generates a shortcut knowledge base; a unified baseline agent consumes it) is a sensible way to isolate shortcut quality from the evaluated agent's own capabilities.

The benchmark has substantive scale and detail: 139 tasks across 11 real-world Android apps in an online, dynamic emulator environment, with a curated knowledge base of 88 shortcuts (APIs, deep links, RPA scripts) documented in appendices, per-app task/shortcut breakdowns, and difficulty-level analysis.

The experimental section covers several axes (task type, input modality, base-model strength) and yields interpretable findings, e.g., that shortcut benefits are largest for weaker base models and that agent-generated shortcuts lag predefined ones in robustness (SSR 0.10 for task-level replays).
The failure-case taxonomy (selection/planning, behavioral/adaptation, execution/formulation errors) with concrete traced examples is useful for future work on shortcut-augmented agents.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not established. The abstract states 'The project page is available at' followed by an empty link, and no artifact (code, task definitions, knowledge base, evaluation harness) is verifiably released. For a benchmark paper, this is a serious deficiency.

Statistical rigor is weak. All headline experiments appear to be single runs on a commercial, non-deterministic model (Gemini-2.5-Pro), with no repeated trials, variance estimates, or significance tests. Key claims such as T3A 51.1% -> MAS-T3A 57.6% on 92 single-app tasks correspond to roughly 6 additional successes and could plausibly be within run-to-run noise.

Table 1, the positioning comparison against AndroidArena/AndroidWorld/LlamaTouch/AndroidLab/SPA-Bench, is self-serving and poorly operationalized: the check/cross criteria for 'difficulty level', 'diverse shortcuts', and 'efficiency & cost metrics' are not defined or justified, and several existing benchmarks plausibly satisfy the marked capabilities. The 'first benchmark' claim is likewise overstated given prior work on skill/shortcut learning and evaluation (e.g., MobileAgent-E, AppAgentX, SkillWeaver).

The benchmark design risks confounding. Predefined shortcuts are hand-crafted with a perfect 100% SSR, and the shortcut knowledge base is injected directly into the baseline agent; the measured 'hybrid agent' gains may largely reflect the quality of hand-engineered tooling rather than the agent's decision-making, which the paper claims to evaluate. The distinction between evaluating shortcut *use* vs. shortcut *availability* is not clearly disentangled.

The shortcut-generation evaluation is thin: it uses only one generating agent (M3A) on a 50% task subset, with three ad hoc generation schemes (task replay, subtask replay, dynamic) that were constructed via prompting; it validates the benchmark's discriminative ability only weakly and does not evaluate any representative learning-based shortcut-generation method.

Metric definitions and reporting are confusing or inconsistent: MSC is marked as higher-is-better without justification; the GSAR description in Sec. 3.6 contradicts itself (a high GUI-to-shortcut ratio is described as evidence of efficient shortcut use); MSR is defined in Sec. 3.6 but tables report MSRS without a precise definition of 'optimal' step counts; the Human baseline rows are largely empty.

Reliability of the automated success evaluation (adapted from SPA-Bench, described as 'embedding shortcut action descriptions') is not validated; no human agreement study or verification audit is reported, which matters for a benchmark whose success rates are the primary evidence.

Writing quality issues undermine clarity: a broken citation '(et al. 2024)', cross-app MobileAgent-E SR of 0.064 with an odd MET (469s for a near-zero success rate) left unexplained, figure/caption errors (e.g., 'Booking_open_shorts()' used in a YouTube task in Fig. 7), and inconsistent notation throughout.

Coverage is narrow: only two proprietary Gemini models and four/three agent frameworks; no open-weight models, and the authors themselves acknowledge the limited baseline range, limiting the benchmark's demonstrated generality.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: no existing benchmark systematically evaluates GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, and the paper clearly motivates why efficiency and mode-selection (GUI vs. shortcut) deserve dedicated evaluation.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: tasks are solvable via GUI-only operations but accelerated by shortcuts, and the knowledge base is intentionally incomplete, forcing agents to plan hybrid solutions rather than rely purely on shortcut replay.

The two-stage shortcut-generation evaluation framework (generation agent builds a knowledge base, which is then imported into a fixed baseline agent) is a clever, isolating methodology that fairly measures shortcut quality independently of the generating agent's intrinsic ability.
The seven metrics (SR, MS, MSRS, MET, MToC, MSC, SSR, GSAR) provide a multi-dimensional view of effectiveness, efficiency, and cost, going beyond simple success rate.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: multiple baseline agents (T3A, M3A, MobileAgentV2, MobileAgent-E), two hybrid variants with different perception modalities (UI tree vs. screenshot), two base models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash), and differentiated analyses by task difficulty and single-app vs. cross-app splits.

Findings are concrete and informative: shortcuts help more for weaker models, predefined shortcuts outperform all agent-generated variants in robustness (SSR 100% vs. 10-75%), and a structured bad-case taxonomy (selection/planning, behavioral/adaptation, execution/formulation errors) adds diagnostic value.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with the main claims supported by tables in the main text and supplementary detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is seriously undermined: the abstract states 'The project page is available at' with no URL, and there is no explicit statement of code, data, task list, or knowledge base release. For a benchmark paper, public availability of the environment, tasks, and evaluator is essential, and its absence is a major concern.

The automated success evaluation is only vaguely described ('we adapt the methodology from SPA-Bench, embedding shortcut action descriptions'); the reliability and validity of the checker are not analyzed (no human verification of auto-evaluation agreement, no discussion of false positives/negatives).

Experimental rigor has gaps: results are from single runs with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the shortcut-generation evaluation uses only a 50% task subset with limited justification; and the 'randomly selected' subset is not characterized against the full distribution.

The benchmark's own evaluative framework is validated mostly through the authors' constructed shortcut-generation methods (replay variants, dynamic shortcuts, MobileAgent-E) rather than through a genuinely diverse set of learning-based generation approaches, so claims about SG capability are only partially demonstrated.

Baseline coverage is thin in the hybrid space: beyond MobileAgent-E, no recent self-evolving/skill-acquisition systems (e.g., AppAgentX, SkillWeaver-style approaches) are evaluated despite being cited as related work, limiting the benchmark's demonstrated discriminative power.

Some results are hard to interpret and not fully explained: e.g., MAS-MobileAgent's MET (682s) is far worse than baselines yet SSR/MSRS improve; T3A's SR on Level 3 (42.9%) exceeds Level 2 (34.8%), an anomaly left unexamined. Efficiency gains vs. success gains are conflated in places.

Table 1's comparison criteria (DS, DL, EC, SG) are defined in a way that favors the proposed benchmark; the claim of being the 'first' benchmark for hybrid mobile agents is asserted rather than rigorously defended against, e.g., AndroidWorld's programmatic task actions or SPA-Bench's scriptable evaluations.

External validity is limited: 139 tasks, 11 apps, a single emulator configuration, and a shortcut knowledge base hand-crafted by the authors; the risk that task design is biased toward the authors' predefined shortcut set (tasks were designed knowing the shortcuts) is acknowledged implicitly ('usable shortcuts exist within our established knowledge base for each task') but not mitigated or analyzed.

Minor quality issues: broken citation ('(et al. 2024)'), Figure 7 labels shortcuts as 'Booking.open_shorts()' for YouTube (inconsistent), and some appendix tables (e.g., Table 8 vs. Figure 6 counts) require careful cross-checking.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: there is currently no benchmark that systematically evaluates GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents or the quality of agent-generated shortcuts, and the paper positions this clearly against prior work (AndroidWorld, SPA-Bench, MobileAgentBench, UFO2, AppAgentX, MobileAgent-E).

The benchmark design is thoughtful: 139 tasks across 11 real-world applications with single-app/cross-app splits, an intentionally incomplete shortcut knowledge base that forces hybrid planning, incremental task variations that test shortcut abstraction, and a documented human step-count baseline collected from three annotators with a defined minimum-step protocol.

The shortcut-generation evaluation protocol is methodologically sound: importing agent-generated shortcut knowledge bases into a fixed baseline executor (T3A) cleanly decouples shortcut quality from the generating agent's intrinsic abilities, and comparing replay, dynamic, and MobileAgent-E shortcuts against a predefined upper bound yields interpretable results (e.g., SSR of 10% for task-level replay vs. 100% for predefined).

Broad empirical coverage: agentic workflows (T3A, M3A, MobileAgentV2), multiple Agent-as-a-Model families across scales (Qwen3-VL 4B–235B, GLM-4.5V, ScaleCUA, MAI-UI), and two base LLMs, with per-category and per-difficulty breakdowns in the appendix.

Honest reporting of negative results (ScaleCUA variants rarely benefit; Qwen3-VL-4B efficiency degrades), shortcut misuse/interference experiments (Tables 11–12), and a reliability study of the automated judge against 278 human-annotated trajectories (F1 96.3%, precision 98.1%).

Reproducibility is addressed at the environment level: snapshot-based AVD reset, dedicated test accounts to isolate side effects, ADB port isolation for parallel execution, and shortcuts restricted to intent-accessible endpoints requiring no root or system modification.
weaknesses: No statistical rigor around the headline comparisons: there is no evidence of multiple runs, seeds, or significance testing, yet many claimed gains are modest (e.g., MAS-Qwen3-VL-4B +3.9% SR, ScaleCUA differences within noise), and some shortcut-augmented variants perform worse than their baselines, making variance assessment essential.

Heavy dependence on an LLM-as-a-Judge for the binary success verdict introduces a potentially correlated bias across all reported numbers, especially since all agents (including the judge's own family, Gemini) were evaluated under the same judge; the human validation covers only one agent (MAS-MobileAgent) on 278 trajectories, so the F1 may not transfer to other agents' failure modes.

Reproducibility of the artifact itself is unclear: the abstract's 'Project page:' entry is empty, and there is no explicit commitment to releasing the code, task definitions, shortcut knowledge base, or MAS-Bench-AVD image; moreover, reliance on live online apps (Amazon, YouTube, Gmail) means content drift could erode comparability even with snapshots.

Metric presentation is confusing and possibly inconsistent: Table 2's efficiency column is labeled 'MSRS' but is discussed as mean steps; Fig. 5 and Tables 9–10 mix MSR/MSRS semantics; several efficiency/cost deltas use inconsistent directions (e.g., token cost 'reduced from 156.441k to 130.980k' framed as an improvement while some table entries mark token-cost reductions in red as regressions).

The shortcut injection mechanism is a keyword-based retrieval over a small, app-scoped pool of 88 shortcuts with shortcut signatures placed directly into prompts; this essentially hints at solutions, and the paper's claims about 'autonomous discovery' would be more convincing with a retrieval-free or distractor-rich default setting rather than a supplementary interference study.

Benchmarks of this kind hinge on artifact release and community adoption; the shortcut stability analysis (five app versions over six months) is reassuring but only briefly reported, and the limitation to an emulator (Pixel 7, Android 15) with a single-screen configuration limits generalization to real devices, which the authors acknowledge.

Writing quality issues: incomplete project page, several references with implausible future arXiv identifiers/years (e.g., 2026 entries, arXiv:2604.09455), and duplicated template text ('For the 92 single-app tasks... For the 47 cross-app tasks') in Appendix A.5.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: MAS-Bench is the first benchmark explicitly designed for GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, with a well-motivated focus on both shortcut *use* and shortcut *generation* — the latter being a novel and forward-looking evaluation problem.

The benchmark is thoughtfully constructed: 139 tasks across 11 real-world apps, 88 predefined shortcuts (APIs, deep-links, RPA scripts), an intentionally incomplete knowledge base that forces hybrid planning, incremental task variations that test shortcut abstraction, and difficulty stratification.

Evaluation infrastructure is unusually rigorous for a benchmark paper: a two-stage Describe-and-Judge automated evaluator validated against 278 human-annotated trajectories (F1 96.3%, precision 98.1%), plus a snapshot-based reset mechanism, isolated test accounts, and side-effect mitigation for reproducibility and ethics.

Experiments are extensive and diverse: agentic workflows (T3A, M3A, MobileAgentV2/E), Agent-as-a-Model variants across multiple model families and scales (Qwen3-VL 4B–235B, GLM-4.5V), and specialized GUI models, with matched GUI-only vs. hybrid comparisons yielding clear headline results (e.g., 35.2%→63.3% SR for MAS-MobileAgent, +79.8% relative).

The findings are nuanced and analytically valuable rather than only leaderboard-style: shortcut gains are non-monotonic in model scale, generalize across perception modalities, specialized GUI models fail to exploit shortcuts, and the interference/no-relevant-shortcut protocol (Table 12) exposes shortcut misuse, demonstrating the benchmark's diagnostic capability.

The shortcut-generation evaluation design — importing generated shortcut knowledge bases into a unified baseline executor — is a clean, executor-controlled protocol that credibly isolates generation quality from executor ability, and the results (replay SSR 10% vs. predefined 100%) yield actionable insights (coordinate-free dynamic shortcuts are more robust).

Detailed appendices (action space, shortcut collection methodology, shortcut stability testing across five app versions over six months, human baseline methodology, bad-case taxonomy) substantially support soundness and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not fully assured in the manuscript: the project page URL is blank, and there is no explicit statement of public release of the tasks, shortcut knowledge base, MAS-Bench-AVD image, and evaluation code; for a benchmark paper this is a significant gap.

The LLM-as-judge reliability study is validated only on trajectories from a single agent (MAS-MobileAgent); agreement may not transfer to other agents' error patterns, and the judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) shares a family with the base models used in agentic workflows, raising possible bias concerns that are not analyzed.

No variance reporting or statistical significance testing: online experiments with dynamic apps are inherently noisy (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-3B vs. 7B ordering anomalies, small SR deltas like MAS-Qwen3-VL-4B +3.9%), so several fine-grained claims (Finding 3) would benefit from multiple runs or confidence intervals.

The 'autonomous discovery' claim is partially undercut by the evaluation setup: keyword-based, application-scoped shortcut retrieval injects only applicable shortcuts into the prompt, removing the retrieval/discovery burden; the open-domain retrieval case is deferred to future work, so the benchmark tests selection and invocation more than discovery.

MToC is missing ('-') for all Agent-as-a-Model variants, limiting the cost analysis for a large portion of Table 2; MET as an efficiency metric is also potentially confounded by network latency and API variability across models.

The main results use only 50% of tasks for the shortcut-generation study (69 tasks) and 23 tasks for the interference study; these small subsets make several conclusions (e.g., 10% SSR for replay-task, -66.67% SR drop) sensitive to a few task outcomes.

Terminology and branding are somewhat confusing: 'MAS-Bench' for a mobile GUI benchmark reads as 'Multi-Agent System' benchmark; also Table 1's 'difficulty level' column comparison and some figures (Fig. 5 labels) are hard to parse.

Scale of the benchmark (139 tasks, 11 apps) is modest relative to AndroidWorld/SPA-Bench; while justified by depth, the paper could be more explicit about coverage limitations (no real devices, Android 15 emulator only, acknowledged in Limitations).
Some referenced works and arXiv IDs appear inconsistent or likely erroneous (e.g., 2026 citations such as arXiv:2604.09455), suggesting citation hygiene issues that should be fixed.
